classes_note: Four classes: (1) field histories of literature and computation, the exhibit's own self-description (B3, B2) and the census's area 'field-history'; (2) algorithmic composition and writing machines before machine learning, from the exhibit's first story and holdings (B3, B2; census record.makes, holdings); (3) algorithmic analysis of literature, the exhibit's second story (B3; census holdings); (4) the procedural lineage of #186, membership by the census's tll_reading for the entity. The aliases are the exhibit's names (The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence; The Literary History of AI; Literary AI, case-sensitive; its host literaryai.library.columbia.edu) and RBML, the census kind's abbreviation of its holder, case-sensitive. Columbia University, its English Department, the Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Digital Scholarship, the CU Narrative Intelligence Lab and the curators named on a card (Alex Gil, Melina Moe, Dennis Yi Tenen) are entities distinct from the exhibit and are not aliases; the general history of AI in literature and fiction that the composition answers (the topic named by the exhibit's title; Cambridge's AI Narratives programme, card 1) is a neighbouring entity and not a class of the exhibit. #186 (Who Is Writing for the Machines?) and #1543 (Generative Uptake), the census's anchors, are read at the passages bearing on the entity's kind: training corpora, writing addressed to a machine reader, machine composition, field histories of electronic and generative literature. Admission by reading (§3.4): D where a deposit names the entity and says something of it; R where it states a relation between the entity and an archive object; O-class where a sentence applies an archive category to one of the four classes; a bare mention, a citation line or a list of keywords is not a claim.
